chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said:

I asked him about the error (killing) in which there is blood money and expiation — is it that one intends to strike a man but does not intend to kill him? He said: Yes. I said: (What about one who) shot at a sheep but hit a human being? He said: That is the error in which there is no doubt — upon him is the blood money and the expiation.

key_terms.الخطأ: Erroneous killing (khata') — one of three categories of homicide in Islamic law: deliberate ('amd), quasi-deliberate (shibh al-'amd), and erroneous (khata')
key_terms.الدية: Diyah (blood money) — compensation paid to the victim's family in cases of homicide or bodily harm
key_terms.الكفارة: Kaffara (expiation) — a religious act of atonement, in this context freeing a slave, fasting two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor persons

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings on erroneous killing requiring both blood money and expiation in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) defines two categories of erroneous killing (khata') that incur both blood money (diyah) and expiation (kaffara): first, intentionally striking a person without intending to kill them; and second, accidentally harming a person while aiming at an animal. The questioner presents a case distinguishing deliberate striking (without lethal intent) from a purely accidental scenario (shooting at a sheep that hits a person), and the Imam affirms that both situations constitute unambiguous error requiring full legal remedies under Islamic law (4:92).
